Breaking the Silence on Urinary Incontinence in Women
Urinary incontinence—the unintentional leakage of urine—is an incredibly common condition, yet it remains widely underreported due to embarrassment or anxiety. Many women silently allow it to compromise their quality of life, social freedom, and confidence.
It is important to know that you do not have to just "live with it." It is a highly treatable medical condition.
🔍 Understanding the Common Types:
1.	Stress Incontinence: Leakage triggered by physical pressure like coughing, sneezing, laughing, or exercising.
2.	Urge Incontinence (Overactive Bladder): A sudden, intense urge to urinate followed by involuntary leakage.
3.	Mixed Incontinence: A combination of both stress and urge symptoms.
4.	Overflow Incontinence: Frequent or constant dribbling because the bladder doesn't empty completely.
⚡ Why Does It Happen?
Key risk factors include pelvic floor weakness or tissue changes caused by childbirth, pregnancy, menopause (due to lower estrogen levels), pelvic surgery, chronic coughing, or natural aging.
🛑 When to Consult a Gynaecologist:
•	If leakage interferes with your daily routines or social activities.
•	If symptoms worsen following childbirth or menopause.
•	If you experience repeated Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs).
•	If you experience pelvic pressure or a visible bulge (signs of pelvic organ prolapse).

Navigating Menopause: Embracing the Next Chapter of Your Health 🌸
Menopause is a completely natural transition marking the end of a woman’s reproductive years, officially diagnosed after 12 consecutive months without a period. While it is a normal biological milestone, the accompanying drop in estrogen and progesterone levels can bring noticeable changes to your body and mind.
Common Signs of the Transition:
•	Vasomotor Shifts: Sudden hot flashes, night sweats, and disrupted sleep patterns.
•	Physical Changes: Vaginal dryness, discomfort during intimacy, and slowed metabolism leading to weight gain.
•	Mood & Cognitive Shifts: Unexplained mood swings, increased anxiety, or temporary "brain fog" and memory lapses.
•	Silent Health Risks: Increased rate of bone thinning (osteoporosis) and cardiovascular shifts.
How Specialized Care Supports You:
1.	Symptom Management: Personalized evaluation for Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) or non-hormonal medical solutions tailored to your risk factors.
2.	Preventative Screenings: Timely tracking through bone density scans, mammograms, and advanced lipid profiling to protect your heart and bones.
3.	Local Therapies: Targeted restorative solutions for pelvic and vaginal health to eliminate discomfort.
Menopause is not a disease—it is a new phase of life that deserves dedicated, proactive care.

Understanding Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Don't Ignore the Signs 🩺
Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is a serious bacterial infection that spreads from the vagina or cervix upward into the female reproductive organs—including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. Because early symptoms can sometimes be mild or unnoticeable, regular gynecological check-ups are essential.
Common Symptoms:
•	Pelvic Discomfort: Persistent pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis.
•	Abnormal Discharge: Unusual, yellow/greenish, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge.
•	Systemic Signs: Sudden fever accompanied by chills.
•	Pain & Irregularities: Burning during urination, pain during intimacy, or unexpected bleeding between cycles.
Why Prompt Treatment is Essential:
Left untreated, PID can lead to long-term complications, including chronic pelvic pain, tubal scarring, fertility challenges, or a life-threatening ectopic pregnancy.

Severe Period Pain? Understanding 	 & How to Find Relief 🩸
Many women dismiss severe menstrual cramps as "normal," but debilitating pain could be a sign of Endometriosis. This chronic condition occurs when tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside it—commonly on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or other pelvic organs.
During your cycle, this tissue thickens and bleeds, but with no way to exit the body, it causes intense inflammation, painful cysts, and scar tissue (adhesions).
Symptoms to Never Ignore:
•	Severe Menstrual Cramps: Pain that isn't relieved by standard painkillers.
•	Chronic Pelvic Pain: Discomfort before, during, or throughout the entire month.
•	Pain During Intercourse: Deep pelvic pain during or after intimacy.
•	Digestive Pain: Painful bowel movements or urination, especially during your period.
•	Fertility Challenges: Difficulty conceiving or unexplained infertility.

featured_reviews.name: Sneha Dey
featured_reviews.review_text:
TL;DR: A deeply disappointing and distressing experience — sharing this in the interest of women considering her as their OB-GYN, especially during pregnancy.

This is my first-ever negative review for a healthcare provider, and I do not write this lightly.

I am currently 7 months pregnant and visited Dr. Anjali after my routine growth scan on May 15 showed that my AFI was “normal to low” (borderline). My regular gynecologist — a highly reputed senior doctor from Hinduja — was out of town and advised me to consult Dr. Anjali instead of waiting a week.

At no point was I panicking. I was simply following medical advice.

Before visiting, I had a brief phone conversation with Dr. Anjali and shared my report with her on WhatsApp. Despite the report not indicating an emergency, she insisted I come to her clinic that very evening instead of the next day.

I complied.

During the consultation, all my vitals were normal. As part of sharing my pregnancy history, I methodically showed her all my ultrasounds from the last 7 months — around 10 in total — including scans that were medically advised due to:

- a hematoma/bleeding episode,
- reduced fetal movement,
- and a fetal echo concern.

I also mentioned — very matter-of-factly — that my baby was measuring around the 10th percentile. This was shared purely as history, not from a place of anxiety or distress.

What followed was nearly 40 minutes of what felt less like a medical consultation and more like unsolicited psychological evaluation.

Dr. Anjali repeatedly interpreted my medical history as evidence of “panic” and “mental distress,” implying:

- that the number of ultrasounds reflected my anxiety,
- and that mentioning my baby’s percentile reflected my “ignorance” about genetics.

I was stunned.

At no point did she ask for context behind the scans or attempt to understand why they had been medically recommended. Instead, she seemed to reduce valid medical history into a narrative about an “overanxious mother.”

She then shifted into giving extended commentary on maternal mental health and how a mother’s mindset affects the fetus. While that may generally be true, I found it deeply inappropriate that she casually arrived at conclusions about my mental state without basis, context, or qualification.

The most disturbing moment came when she asked whether I take protein powder regularly. I honestly replied that there are days I skip it because it causes nausea and constipation.

To this, she jokingly suggested to my husband that he should give me a “laafa” (slap) because I was “behaving like a child.”

I want to repeat this clearly:
A practicing gynecologist — and someone who claims to counsel women emotionally — suggested physical violence, even if “as a joke,” during a pregnancy consultation.

It was not funny.

Pregnancy is already physically and emotionally demanding. Women constantly navigate fear, societal pressure, medical uncertainty, and vulnerability. The last thing a patient needs is to feel mocked, patronized, psychologically analysed without consent, or shamed for responsibly sharing medical history.

What saddened me most was not just the lack of empathy, but the normalization of such behaviour by another woman doctor.

Patients deserve:

- respect,
- informed medical guidance,
- emotional safety,
- and the freedom to ask questions or share concerns without being trivialized.

A consultation should never leave a pregnant woman feeling humiliated, dismissed, or emotionally exhausted.

Dr. Anjali, if you are reading this: empathy is not optional in healthcare. And if mental health is something you wish to advise patients on, perhaps begin with understanding boundaries, sensitivity, and dignity.

If not, please stick to obstetrics.

PMOS is not just about “cysts” in the ovaries. It is a hormonal and metabolic condition that can affect periods, weight, acne, facial hair, insulin resistance, fertility and long-term health. The treatment approach remains the same, but the new name encourages a more complete evaluation of hormones, insulin, thyroid, lipids and overall metabolic health.  

You should consider seeing a gynaecologist if you have:

- Irregular or absent periods
- Acne or excess facial hair
- Unexplained weight gain
- Difficulty conceiving
 - A previous PCOS diagnosis without recent follow-up
